criterion_notes.c1: Although primarily a watershed-scale glaciology, hydrology, and multi-sector water-resources study (covering agricultural irrigation, hydropower, and mining), the paper includes household-level residential drinking-water components: a 911-household survey of urban residential water supply continuity in Huancayo and a 125-household survey in three upper Santa sub-catchments reporting water shortages for direct household consumption as well as irrigation.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is NO: the empirical household water-access components examine biophysical glacier recession, catchment glacierization, and spatial proximity to springs/streams rather than any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household or community water/sanitation service access (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation rules, tariffs, enforcement/disconnection, or utility governance). Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the study is also EXCLUDE (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude): while Section 4.3.3 narratively synthesizes prior research on watershed councils, ad-hoc drought contingencies, payments for ecosystem services (Law No. 30215), and formalization of volumetric water-use rights under Peru's 2009 Hydrologic Resources Law (PROFODUA), those discussions concern basin-scale water-resource management and agricultural/industrial irrigation entitlements rather than household drinking-water or sanitation service access, and no governance factor is empirically linked to the household service-access outcomes.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary and synthesized empirical evidence, including hydrological/glaciological field measurements, Landsat land-cover change detection (1990-2011), a stratified random survey of 125 households in three Santa River sub-catchments, 10 semi-structured interviews in the Shullcas watershed, and a survey of 911 urban households in Huancayo.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household water-access outcomes including daily hours of residential water access in Huancayo (<50% with 20-24 hours/day; ~20% with <10 hours/day) and household-reported dry-season water shortages for direct consumption (<10%) and irrigation (~25%) in upper Santa catchments.
criterion_notes.c5: The study's populations and units of analysis (households and watersheds), biophysical exposures (glacier recession and % catchment glacierization), water availability/continuity outcomes, and mixed-methods case-study/synthesis design are identifiable, though no legal/administrative exposure is linked to household service access.

evidence_quotes.quote: In this paper, we develop and apply a conceptual framework focusing on these multiple dimensions of water access through the integration and synthesis of results from a long-term transdisciplinary research collaboration with new findings from two glacierized watersheds in the Peruvian Andes.

The surveys were conducted in 2008 and 2009 and yielded a statistically significant and representative sample comprised of 125 households (40 from Querococha, 32 from Quilcay, and 53 from Llanganuco) that included 543 people (Bury et al., 2011; Mark et al., 2010).
An additional survey of urban residential water access was carried out in 911 households within the city of Huancayo during December, 2015.

Across all areas surveyed, less than 10 % of respondents indicated water shortages for direct consumption during recent dry seasons, while approximately 25% reported shortages for irrigation water (cf. Mark et al., 2010).

Surveys of more than 900 households in Huancayo in 2015 revealed that less than 50% had constant (20-24 hours per day) access to water while approximately 20% had less than 10 hours of water access per day (Fig. 7).

In the Santa watershed, some rural, upper-basin irrigators have refused to register for formalized rights, instead insisting that the government uphold their customary uses (PROFODUA, 2011). Others have accepted formal allocations but find their volumetric character abstract and lacking impact on quotidian water management (Parón-Llullán, 2011).

raw_response.exposure: Climate-driven glacier recession and proglacial hydrologic transformation (varying catchment glacierization and groundwater-surface water dynamics), alongside descriptive watershed-level economic, infrastructure, and water-resource governance context
raw_response.outcome: Perceived dry-season water declines and water shortages for direct household consumption and irrigation (Santa sub-catchments); daily hours of urban residential water supply (Huancayo); and basin-scale water availability, quality, and sectoral withdrawals
raw_response.population_and_sample: Santa River and Shullcas River watersheds in the Peruvian Andes: 125 rural/peri-urban households (543 individuals) in three upper Santa sub-catchments (Querococha n=40, Quilcay n=32, Llanganuco n=53; 2008-2009), 911 urban residential households in Huancayo (December 2015), 10 key-informant interviewees in the Shullcas watershed (2014-2015), plus key informants in the Santa watershed
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). This transdisciplinary study synthesizes glaciological, hydrological, land-cover, and social research on climate-driven glacier recession and basin-scale water resources in two Peruvian watersheds (Santa and Shullcas). Although it reports descriptive household water-supply outcomes (daily hours of urban residential water access across 911 households in Huancayo and perceived dry-season shortages for direct consumption across 125 households in upper Santa catchments), the exposure examined in relation to household water access is biophysical/hydrologic change (glacier loss, streamflow variability, and spatial location relative to springs/streams), not a legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism governing service access. Its narrative section on water rights and governance (Section 4.3.3) synthesizes prior work on basin-scale watershed councils and volumetric water-rights formalization for agricultural/industrial river users (PROFODUA under the 2009 Hydrologic Resources Law) rather than any rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access, and does not empirically link any governance exposure to residential service-access outcomes.
raw_response.study_design: Mixed-methods transdisciplinary case study and synthesis (combining glaciological/hydrological measurements, remote-sensing land-cover analysis, stratified household surveys, semi-structured interviews, and institutional/archival review)
